summary.text: An inequality is a relation that makes a non-equal comparison between two numbers or other mathematical expressions.
Its main types are less than and greater than, written < and >, and in either case a is not equal to b.
Adding or subtracting the same number preserves an inequality, while multiplying or dividing by a negative constant reverses it.

facts.label: Strict symbols
facts.value: < and > mean strictly less or strictly greater

facts.label: Non-strict symbols
facts.value: a ≤ b means a is at most b

facts.label: Wallis, 1670
facts.value: Used a single horizontal bar above < and >

facts.label: Bouguer, 1734
facts.value: ≦ and ≧ first appeared in his work

facts.label: Chained form
facts.value: a < b < c stands for a < b and b < c

items.prompt: You know that 2 < 5. You multiply both sides by −3. What is true afterwards?
items.explain: Multiplying by a negative constant reverses the inequality relation, so the sign flips.

items.prompt: You know that a < b. A friend adds 7 to both sides. What happens to the relation?
items.explain: The inequality relation is preserved under addition (or subtraction).

items.prompt: A sign says a < b. Which statement says exactly the same thing from the other side?
items.explain: Reversing the order of the two quantities while flipping the inequality symbol gives an equivalent statement.

items.prompt: A friend says a ≠ b tells you that a is the larger one. What is wrong with that?

options.label: Nothing, it always means a is larger
It means they are equal after all
It says only that they differ, not which is bigger
It means b must be the larger one

items.explain: The notation a ≠ b does not say that one is greater than the other, and it does not even require an ordered set.

items.prompt: You read a < b < c. A classmate asks how a compares with c. What can you say?

options.label: a < c, because less-than carries through
a > c, because the order flips
a = c, because b sits between them

items.explain: The chain means a < b and b < c, and by transitivity it also follows that a < c.

items.prompt: You apply a monotonically decreasing function to both sides of a < b. What happens to the inequality?
items.explain: Applying a monotonically decreasing function to both sides reverses the inequality relation.

pack.title: When the sign flips
pack.question: How can you change both sides of an inequality without breaking it?

beats.title: When the sign flips
beats.hook: Multiply by 2 and nothing changes; multiply by −2 and the whole statement turns around.

beats.prompt: You start with 1 < 4 and divide both sides by a negative constant. What should the sign become?
beats.explain: The inequality relation is preserved under division with a positive constant but reversed when a negative constant is involved.

choices.label: Still <
choices.feedback: That would keep the order, but a negative constant reverses it.

choices.label: Now =
choices.feedback: Dividing never makes two different numbers equal.

beats.prompt: match each notation to its meaning

right.label: a is strictly less than b
a is not equal to b

beats.explain: Each symbol names a different comparison between a and b.

beats.prompt: sort each symbol into its group
beats.explain: The non-strict inequalities are ≤ and ≥, and their corresponding strict versions are < and >.

beats.prompt: one step in this reasoning is wrong; which?

steps.text: Subtract 4 from both sides to get −2 < 2.
Multiply both sides by −1 and keep the sign: 2 < −2.

beats.explain: Multiplying by a negative constant reverses the inequality, so the result should be 2 > −2.

beats.idea: Adding the same number keeps an inequality as it is, while multiplying by a negative constant reverses it.

paragraphs.heading: Comparing without equals
paragraphs.text: An inequality compares two numbers or expressions without saying they are equal. Most often it tells you which of two numbers on the number line is bigger. The two main kinds are "less than", written <, and "greater than", written >. With either sign, a and b are not equal, and so these are called strict inequalities.

paragraphs.heading: Or equal to
paragraphs.text: A looser version lets the two sides match. a ≤ b says a is less than or equal to b, in other words at most b, and a ≥ b says a is at least b. A different sign, a ≠ b, says only that a and b differ. It does not say which one is bigger, and a and b need not even belong to a set that has an order.

paragraphs.heading: Moving things around
paragraphs.text: Swapping the two sides while turning the sign around gives the same statement, so a < b and b > a mean the same thing. You can add or subtract the same amount on both sides and the inequality still holds. Multiplying or dividing both sides by a positive constant keeps it as well. Multiplying or dividing by a negative constant reverses it.

paragraphs.heading: Applying a function
paragraphs.text: The same thinking extends to functions. A monotonically increasing function can be applied to both sides without breaking the inequality, as long as both sides lie in its domain. A monotonically decreasing function, by contrast, reverses the inequality. For example, when a and b are positive real numbers you may take the natural logarithm of both sides, because the natural logarithm is strictly increasing.

paragraphs.heading: Chains of inequalities
paragraphs.text: Inequalities can be chained. a < b < c is shorthand for a < b and b < c, and from those two it follows that a < c. You may add or subtract one number in all three parts, or multiply or divide all three by one nonzero number, reversing every sign if that number is negative. So a < b + e < c says the same as a − e < b < c − e.

paragraphs.heading: How the symbols settled
paragraphs.text: The signs took a while to settle. In the 17th and 18th centuries writers used personal notations or typewriter signs. In 1670 John Wallis drew a single horizontal bar above the < and > signs instead of below them. In 1734 the double-barred ≦ and ≧ appeared in the work of Pierre Bouguer, and later mathematicians trimmed these to one bar, ≤, or a slanted one, ⩽.

paragraphs.heading: Much bigger than
paragraphs.text: Engineers also use a less formal sign to say one quantity dwarfs another, normally by several orders of magnitude. The point is that the smaller value can then be dropped from an approximation with little effect on its accuracy.
